job_description:
Software Engineer - Full Stack

We are seeking an experienced Senior Software Engineer to join our dynamic team. The ideal candidate will have:

Requirements:
• 1 years of experience in software development
• Strong proficiency in JavaScript/TypeScript, React, Node.js
• Experience with cloud platforms (AWS, Azure, or GCP)
• Solid understanding of microservices architecture
• Experience with CI/CD pipelines and DevOps practices
• Strong problem-solving and analytical skills
• Excellent communication and teamwork abilities

Responsibilities:
• Design and implement scalable web applications
• Lead technical discussions and code reviews
• Collaborate with product and design teams
• Contribute to architectural decisions

competencies.name: React and JavaScript Fundamentals
competencies.rationale: Given the job requires strong proficiency in React and JavaScript/TypeScript, a behavioral foundation interview style is appropriate to assess the candidate's real-world experience with component architecture, state management, and debugging in React applications. This style evaluates how they've applied these skills in past projects, revealing practical depth and problem-solving under real-time constraints.

competencies.name: Cloud and Microservices Architecture
competencies.rationale: The role emphasizes experience with cloud platforms (AWS, Azure, GCP) and microservices architecture. A system design scaling interview allows candidates to demonstrate their understanding of service decomposition, communication patterns (e.g., APIs, messaging), and scalability trade-offs in distributed systems—critical for a full-stack engineer in a scalable environment.

competencies.name: CI/CD and DevOps Practices
competencies.rationale: This competency focuses on experience with CI/CD pipelines and DevOps practices. A data insight interview enables the evaluation of how candidates have implemented and optimized automated workflows, monitored deployment health, and responded to pipeline failures—providing insight into their operational thinking and data-driven decision-making in deployment processes.

criteria.name: Defines core React concepts in accessible language
criteria.description: Can clearly explain React component lifecycle, state management, and hooks using everyday analogies or real-world examples.

scoring_levels.Level 0: Cannot define core concepts; provides vague or incorrect explanations.
scoring_levels.Level 1: Provides basic definitions but lacks clarity or context; misses key components like hooks or lifecycle.
scoring_levels.Level 2: Defines core concepts with basic accuracy but lacks practical application or examples.
scoring_levels.Level 3: Clearly explains concepts with relevant examples and links them to real-world use cases.
scoring_levels.Level 4: Explains concepts with depth, including edge cases (e.g., performance implications of useEffect).
scoring_levels.Level 5: Demonstrates deep understanding with nuanced comparisons (e.g., React vs. Vue, useEffect vs. useState).

criteria.name: Applies React concepts to a real-world project scenario
criteria.description: Can describe how they used React components, state, or hooks to solve a specific problem in a past project.

scoring_levels.Level 0: No specific project example; response is generic or non-technical.
scoring_levels.Level 1: Mentions a project but fails to link React features to actual implementation details.
scoring_levels.Level 2: Provides a basic project example with limited technical depth.
scoring_levels.Level 3: Describes a project with clear use of React features (e.g., hooks, state) and problem context.
scoring_levels.Level 4: Details a complex feature (e.g., form validation, dynamic rendering) with React-specific patterns.
scoring_levels.Level 5: Demonstrates advanced pattern usage (e.g., memoization, error boundaries) and debugging in production.

criteria.name: Troubleshoots React issues under time pressure
criteria.description: Can identify and resolve a common React debugging issue (e.g., state mutation, rendering bugs) in a simulated or real scenario.

scoring_levels.Level 0: Fails to identify or resolve issues; provides no debugging process.
scoring_levels.Level 1: Attempts to debug but lacks systematic approach; misses key tools (e.g., React DevTools).
scoring_levels.Level 2: Uses basic debugging tools but misses root cause; provides incomplete solution.
scoring_levels.Level 3: Applies systematic debugging (e.g., inspecting props, useEffects) and identifies a fix.
scoring_levels.Level 4: Diagnoses and resolves a complex issue (e.g., race condition, memory leak) with clear reasoning.
scoring_levels.Level 5: Anticipates edge cases and prevents future bugs through proactive debugging practices.

criteria.name: Designs scalable microservice communication patterns
criteria.description: Can describe how services communicate (APIs, messaging) and how they scale under load.

scoring_levels.Level 0: No understanding of communication patterns; suggests monolithic design.
scoring_levels.Level 1: Lists communication types but does not explain trade-offs or failure modes.
scoring_levels.Level 2: Describes basic patterns (e.g., REST, gRPC) with limited context on scalability.
scoring_levels.Level 3: Explains trade-offs (latency vs. reliability) and applies patterns to a real system.
scoring_levels.Level 4: Proposes a service decomposition with observability and load balancing in mind.
scoring_levels.Level 5: Designs a resilient, fault-tolerant architecture with circuit breakers, retries, and fallbacks.

criteria.name: Identifies and resolves scaling bottlenecks in a system
criteria.description: Can analyze a system and pinpoint a performance or scalability issue and propose a mitigation strategy.

scoring_levels.Level 0: Fails to identify bottlenecks; offers no actionable solution.
scoring_levels.Level 1: Mentions a potential issue but lacks depth or technical justification.
scoring_levels.Level 2: Identifies a bottleneck (e.g., database query) and suggests a simple fix (e.g., index).
scoring_levels.Level 3: Analyzes a bottleneck with data (e.g., latency logs) and proposes a scalable fix (e.g., caching).
scoring_levels.Level 4: Proposes a distributed solution (e.g., offload to a service) with clear trade-offs.
scoring_levels.Level 5: Anticipates cascading failures and includes observability (metrics, logging) in the solution.

criteria.name: Conducts a risk assessment for system failure modes
criteria.description: Can identify failure points (e.g., network partition, data loss) and propose mitigation strategies.

scoring_levels.Level 0: No awareness of failure modes; ignores system resilience.
scoring_levels.Level 1: Lists a few failure types without context or mitigation.
scoring_levels.Level 2: Identifies one failure mode and suggests a basic recovery step.
scoring_levels.Level 3: Discusses multiple failure modes (e.g., network, data) and suggests monitoring or backup.
scoring_levels.Level 4: Proposes automated recovery (e.g., auto-restart, health checks) and alerting strategies.
scoring_levels.Level 5: Designs a comprehensive resilience plan with rollback, failover, and disaster recovery.

criteria.name: Defines a key CI/CD metric and its business impact
criteria.description: Can articulate a key metric (e.g., deployment frequency, lead time) and explain how it affects product delivery or customer experience.

scoring_levels.Level 0: Cannot define a metric; response is vague or irrelevant.
scoring_levels.Level 1: Names a metric but does not link it to business outcomes.
scoring_levels.Level 2: Defines a metric and mentions a basic business impact (e.g., faster releases).
scoring_levels.Level 3: Clearly defines a metric and explains how it improves user experience or reduces risk.
scoring_levels.Level 4: Links metric to customer outcomes (e.g., reduced downtime) and business KPIs.
scoring_levels.Level 5: Justifies metric selection with data and tradeoff analysis (e.g., noise vs. signal).

criteria.name: Walks through a CI/CD experiment and its guardrails
criteria.description: Can describe a real-world CI/CD experiment, including setup, success criteria, and failure recovery steps.

scoring_levels.Level 0: No experiment described; no guardrails or recovery plan.
scoring_levels.Level 1: Mentions a pipeline but lacks detail on experiment or failure handling.
scoring_levels.Level 2: Describes a pipeline with basic success criteria and one failure step.
scoring_levels.Level 3: Details a pipeline with defined success/failure conditions and rollback logic.
scoring_levels.Level 4: Describes a complex experiment (e.g., canary deployment) with rollback and monitoring.
scoring_levels.Level 5: Documents a data-driven experiment with A/B testing, baselines, and bias mitigation.

criteria.name: Justifies tradeoffs in pipeline configuration
criteria.description: Can explain how they balanced speed, reliability, and cost in a CI/CD pipeline design.

scoring_levels.Level 0: No tradeoff analysis; presents a one-sided pipeline design.
scoring_levels.Level 1: Mentions tradeoffs but lacks depth or justification.
scoring_levels.Level 2: Lists a few tradeoffs (e.g., speed vs. testing) with minimal reasoning.
scoring_levels.Level 3: Clearly explains a tradeoff (e.g., faster builds vs. test coverage) and its impact.
scoring_levels.Level 4: Analyzes multiple tradeoffs (e.g., cost, time, stability) and justifies decisions with data.
scoring_levels.Level 5: Anticipates pipeline noise and bias, and proposes mitigation (e.g., test matrix optimization).
